- If sentiment is positive (≥0.2) in recent days, model tends to overestimate; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.0) or neutral, model often overcorrects upward; allow for sharper downward correction or mean reversion bias.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >85), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply lagged mean reversion or reduce forecast slope post-spike.
- When sentiment is low and price is trending down, model often underestimates the drop; adjust downward bias by 5–10% of recent mean.
- Forecast horizon 30d shows persistent overestimation in early periods (first 5–7 days) — apply early correction factor based on sentiment volatility.
- If sentiment history shows repeated 0.50 spikes, model tends to overreact; dampen forecast response to sentiment peaks.
- Mean reversion is stronger in low-sentiment periods — model should revert to 30-day moving average if sentiment <0.1 for 3+ days.
- Overshoots after sentiment spikes are common — apply “cool-down” rule: reduce forecast by 0.5–1.0% per day after sentiment peak.
